title: The benefits of evolving rep ranges
summary: NH explains evolving rep and set ranges (e.g. 3-5 sets of 3-5 reps) versus fixed schemes like 5x5. Evolving ranges give full control over volume, intensity and tonnage, encourage rep or volume PRs every session and avoid hard plateaus. He also notes the risk for lazy lifters and says fixed and evolving ranges work best combined.

claims.claim: Most bodybuilding principles are simple; if one seems complex, something about it is probably misunderstood, though simple topics branch out endlessly.
5x5 is a fixed rep range: hit 5 reps on all 5 sets, then add weight. The evolving version would be 3-5 sets of 3-5 reps.
About 95% of his training uses evolving rep ranges.
Evolving rep and set ranges let you control intensity through reps and volume through sets, so the final tonnage depends on your will and needs.
Fixed schemes give a fixed tonnage; if you miss it you must repeat it, which he sees as a problem. He considers 5x5 and 10x10 conservative, orthodox schemes that usually aren't best.
Evolving ranges can be dangerous for novices or lazy people, who will always pick the minimum, but such people don't make it on fixed schemes either.
His philosophy: strength work first at lower reps, then more volume with variations, isolations and accessories.
Example: he benches 4 reps one day, then four days later gets 5 and 4 with an extra set, earning a rep PR on maximal strength plus extra volume.
PRs aren't essential for bodybuilding, but knowing you're getting stronger helps mentally.
On 5x5 or 10x10, once you plateau you plateau hard and may even regress, which hurts tonnage and size.
If you target 6 reps and stall at 4, an evolving range lets you add sets (4,4,4) and still get a volume PR.
Training should be freedom: neither winging it nor treating your program like the Ten Commandments; flexibility is needed even for neurotic people.
Fixed rep ranges still have a use, but only alongside evolving ones; together they pair an immovable object with a flexible value.
Evolving rep ranges aren't suitable for beginners but give supreme volume and intensity control to those who master them.
